mcqs.question: In cache-aside, what happens on the very first request for a key that's never been cached before?
options: It always misses, falls through to the database, and the app writes the result into the cache for next time
It's served from the cache instantly, since the cache pre-loads all possible keys
It fails with an error, since cache-aside requires the key to already exist in the cache
It's served from the database every time, and the cache is never populated automatically
mcqs.explanation: Cache-aside only ever holds what's been explicitly requested, so a brand-new key always misses first, then gets backfilled by the app after the database read. It doesn't pre-load, doesn't error on a miss, and does get populated automatically as part of the read path.

mcqs.question: A write-behind cache node crashes 2 seconds after accepting a write, before that write has been flushed to the database. What happens to that write?
options: The database automatically recovers it from its own write-ahead log
It's permanently lost — the database never received it and has no record of it
It's retried automatically once the cache node restarts
Nothing — write-behind guarantees durability equal to write-through
mcqs.explanation: Write-behind returns success before the database write happens, so any data that existed only in the crashed cache node is gone for good — the database has no record to recover, and there's no automatic retry across a crash. This is exactly the trade-off write-behind makes for speed, unlike write-through, which is durable by the time it returns.

mcqs.question: A team needs the cache and database to never disagree, even briefly, and can accept somewhat slower writes. Which pattern fits best?
options: Write-behind, since it keeps the cache maximally up to date
Cache-aside, since it's the simplest option
Write-through, since the write only completes once both the cache and database are updated together
Read-through, since it handles all writes automatically
mcqs.explanation: Write-through's defining trait is synchronously writing to both cache and database before returning, which is exactly what "never disagree" requires — at the cost of slower writes, which the team said they can accept. Write-behind is the opposite of consistent (data can be lost or lag). Cache-aside can have a brief staleness window. Read-through only addresses the read path, not writes.

mcqs.question: Which kind of data is write-behind caching most appropriate for?
options: Payment transaction records, since speed matters most for money movement
Order confirmation records, since customers expect instant writes
User account passwords, since they change infrequently
A high-throughput view counter, where losing a few seconds of increments in a rare crash is acceptable
mcqs.explanation: A view counter can tolerate losing a handful of increments in a rare crash, which is exactly write-behind's trade-off. Payments and order confirmations are precisely the data that must never be lost, making write-behind's durability gap unacceptable there — write-through or synchronous writes fit those better. Password change frequency isn't the relevant factor.
